edi_broker.text: Good day. Shares for the prudent investor. And for the other sort, at the same commission.

edi_saver.text: Spread your money about, buy good companies, and leave them be. Dividends every quarter. Dull, but dull pays.
Now that Doggerel nonsense down in London? Aye, I'll pass. A coin about a dog. Away wi' ye.

else.text: A member and a Scot with a plan. A business plan for a community buyout? Splendid. Sums first, sentiment second. Ask the auctioneer how the Enclosure sells.

guild_traders.text: Buy low, sell high, and keep the receipts.

else.text: A Highland estate called Dunmaol? Ben Lee grazing, a lodge, a township with a roof or two. The Enclosure's liquidator is selling it and has not mentioned the community right to buy. Funny that.
You can watch a sale for the price of a seat. Take a look.

edi_auctioneer.text: Lots from the Enclosure's estate, once the Moot's had its say. Real hills, real woods, real bog, and a reserve on each. Care to see the catalogue?

then.text: I rang 159 in the end. A very nice person confirmed it was nonsense and asked if I'd been sitting down. I had not.

else.text: I've just had a call. 'The fraud team at your bank.' Knew my name and the last four digits of my card. They said my account was under attack and I should move my money to a safe account.
I nearly did. Then they asked me to read out the code they'd just texted me, and something went cold.

options: Read the code, it's only six digits
Moved the money, they sounded very official

then.text: Never. That code is the key to the door. Handing it over is handing over the money, and banks say so in every leaflet.
Right. Hang up, give it a few minutes (some scammers keep the line open), then ring 159 or the number on your card. 159 puts you through to your own bank, and most of the big ones are on it.
No bank in the world has a 'safe account' for you to move money to. That phrase is the scam.

else.text: The caller knew his name and part of his card number. That proves nothing, because scammers buy leaked details. The number on screen proves nothing either, as it can be faked.
So the rule is simple. They called you, so you don't trust them. Hang up and call your bank back yourself.
I told the bank. They froze it before a penny moved. Take this. My nan swore by it for shock.
Noted in the Almanac under Things worth knowing.
